title: Nepal’s Struggle for a More Resilient Future - The Colgate Maroon-News
description: Nepal’s Struggle for a More Resilient Future  The Colgate Maroon-News
publisher.title: The Colgate Maroon-News
full_article:
Growing up, my home country was never in the news. In fact, I often doubted whether people knew where Nepal was. That has changed recently. Over the past year, Nepal has found itself in the international spotlight. First, as young people took to the streets in what was dubbed the “Gen-Z” revolution, and now as floods devastate the country.

Last September, images appeared of young Nepalis filling the streets. What started with anger over the government’s decision to restrict social media quickly grew into a much larger movement against corruption, unemployment and political dysfunction. The protests eventually forced Prime Minister K. P. Sharma Oli from office.

Now, a year later, Nepal is back in the headlines, this time for a different reason. Floodwaters have destroyed homes and infrastructure, killed over 1,000 people and left thousands more missing. These floods are exposing another side of the same struggle faced a year ago, forcing us to confront what happens when a country with limited resources, fragile infrastructure and political corruption faces a crisis of this scale.

The immediate trigger for the revolution came in September 2025 , when the government restricted access to 26 social media platforms, including Facebook, YouTube and X. For many young Nepalis, the protests represented a demand for greater accountability from a political system that had failed to keep pace with the generation it governed, the government’s inability to repair a collapsing job market, corruption and a poor education system.

That demand for accountability matters even more when looking at Nepal’s response to the floods. More than 25 percent of Nepal’s population lives below the national poverty line. Although poverty has declined significantly since the 1990s, Nepal remains a developing country with major economic and infrastructure inequalities. Rural communities in particular face limited access to roads, healthcare and other basic services. These weaknesses become even more serious when extreme weather strikes.

The floods that struck Nepal on August 26 have killed more than 1,000 people, with many more still missing. Entire communities have been devastated, while roads, bridges and telecommunications networks have been damaged. According to Dharma Raj Upreti , Chief of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, property, housing and infrastructure worth at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees, or approximately $2.56 billion, was lost in the floods. The estimated cost of rebuilding roads and temporary shelters, providing drinking water and restoring electricity is expected to reach around $52.6 million during the first four months of recovery.

The damage has also exposed the vulnerability of Nepal’s strained healthcare system. Seven hospitals and health centres were damaged, while access to others has been restricted by blocked roads. For communities that already struggle to reach healthcare, a destroyed road can determine whether someone gets treatment at all.

Some of these vulnerabilities are avoidable. Narayan Adhikari , Director of Accountability Lab Nepal, argues that political interests often shape infrastructure projects instead of long-term planning. He says building codes and environmental protections are routinely ignored through “cronyism , nepotism and manipulated environmental, social and governance standards.” He points out that hydropower projects are approved without sufficient attention to climate resilience to boost short-term profits and electricity. Almost all of Nepal’s electricity comes from hydropower, with the hydropower plants located high in the mountains. This has had serious consequences for potentially hundreds of hydropower workers believed to be trapped under debris from the floods.

This is particularly concerning as Nepal faces a changing climate. The recent floods were caused by ice breaking from a mountain glacier and flowing into major rivers along the Nepal-Tibet border. Across the Himalayan region, temperatures are rising faster than the global average, increasing the risk of floods, landslides and avalanches.

Additionally, climate change does not affect everyone equally. A wealthy country may have the resources to rebuild quickly, reinforce infrastructure and evacuate vulnerable communities before the disaster. In Nepal that same disaster can have much more devastating consequences.

For Nepal’s new government, the timing could hardly be more difficult. Led by 36-year-old Balendra Shah, the government is now being forced to prove that it can deliver beyond its promises. As The New York Times reports, Shah’s team has already faced tensions over how to balance populist welfare commitments with the austerity measures needed to grow Nepal’s economy. The floods add another dilemma: how can a government with limited resources simultaneously rebuild after a disaster, protect vulnerable communities and deliver the economic change it promised?

title: Humanitarian Needs Grow as Nepal Recovers from Catastrophic Floods - NationofChange
description: Humanitarian Needs Grow as Nepal Recovers from Catastrophic Floods  NationofChange
publisher.title: NationofChange
full_article:
Two weeks after devastating floods struck Nepal, communities across the country are still struggling to meet basic needs as humanitarian efforts continue. The disaster, triggered by a glacial collapse, has become one of Nepal’s deadliest in recent years, leaving widespread destruction in its wake.



As of Wednesday, 1,367 people had been confirmed dead, while 5,132 remained missing, including 587 foreign nationals. 13,646 people have been rescued, but many families are still waiting for news about their loved ones. Search operations remain ongoing, including efforts to reach people who may still be trapped in tunnels and other difficult-to-access areas.

The scale of the destruction has made delivering aid particularly challenging. Floodwaters have damaged homes, roads, bridges, and other essential infrastructure, leaving some communities isolated. The Nepalese government has been using military helicopters to drop aid into areas that remain difficult to reach, while temporary bridges are also being constructed to reconnect communities that have received insufficient assistance.

Families urgently need food, clean drinking water, shelter and access to healthcare. Health services are particularly important for vulnerable groups, including an estimated 1,600 pregnant women who are expected to give birth soon. Ensuring that these women can reach medical facilities and receive appropriate prenatal and emergency care is a major concern.

Mental health support is another pressing need that could become increasingly important as the immediate emergency begins to subside. Survivors have lost homes, livelihoods and, in many cases, family members.

On Wednesday September 9, UN Resident Coordinator for Nepal Lila Pieters Yahia, briefed reporters at UN Headquarters on the ongoing humanitarian efforts by the UN and the Nepalese government.

“People were just so depressed,” Yahia reflected after her visit to the affected communities.

Many people are also coping with the uncertainty of not knowing whether missing relatives are alive. Reuniting separated families and children has therefore become another important part of the humanitarian response.

The United Nations and its humanitarian partners launched a USD 49.6 million flash appeal last Friday to provide life-saving assistance to people affected by the disaster. The appeal is intended to support critical needs including food, clean water, logistics and other immediate relief. So far, approximately USD 22 million has been pledged, leaving a significant funding gap.

The Nepal Red Cross Society is leading much of the humanitarian response, with support from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, the International Committee of the Red Cross and other humanitarian organizations. Aid is being distributed through a combination of government agencies, community organizations and non-governmental organizations. However, humanitarian officials continue to warn that access remains one of the greatest obstacles to reaching people in need.

Yahia described the destruction as an example of the increasingly severe losses faced by countries vulnerable to climate change. “The devastation Nepal has experienced is an extraordinary, stark illustration of the losses and damages that climate-vulnerable countries are increasingly facing,” she said.

Nepal’s experience has also renewed calls for greater international action on climate change and climate justice. As a mountainous country particularly vulnerable to changing weather patterns and the effects of a warming climate, Nepal faces a disproportionate burden.

Despite the enormous challenges, Yahia says aid is reaching many affected communities, and survivors continue to demonstrate hope. “People are still searching for family members they know they may never find,” she said, highlighting the resilience keeping people strong. Yet thousands of people remain in need, and the destruction of transportation networks means that reaching the most isolated communities will take time.

“My plea tonight to the international community: we need to demonstrate solidarity with the people of Nepal,” Yahia emphasized.

For Nepal, the emergency is far from over. The immediate priority remains saving lives and providing food, water, shelter and access to healthcare. As communities begin the long process of rebuilding, the country will also need sustained international support to recover from one of its most destructive disasters.

title: Nepal floods: How measuring snow in the Himalayas could help avoid future disasters - phys.org
description: Nepal floods: How measuring snow in the Himalayas could help avoid future disasters  phys.org
publisher.title: phys.org
full_article:
Credit: Imad Clicks from Pexels

The massive and deadly floods on the Nepal–Tibet border are a stark reminder of why the world needs to constantly update its understanding of the fragile ecosystem in the Himalayas.

These towering mountains contain nearly 90,000 glaciers, which sustain 10 major river systems. Nearby countries, including India, Pakistan, China, Afghanistan, Nepal and Bhutan, rely on water resources that cross borders here. As major river-based hydro economies, their agricultural production, energy security and wider economic stability depend on the availability and timing of river flows.

Changes in snowmelt, glacier retreat and water availability can cause untold hardship for millions of people who rely on them. They can also create incredible danger, as seen in August 2026, when a flash flood caused by a collapsed glacier washed away villages, bridges and roads on both sides of the Tibet–Nepal border, killing more than 1,000 people.

Understanding and measuring winter snowfall in these regions is exceptionally important. It is the main source of freshwater when released by melting snow during the region's warm, early-summer crop-growing seasons, when local communities need it most.

Understanding future Himalayan hazards

No one knows precisely how much water the mountains currently provide or how this will change. This knowledge gap also hinders our understanding of geohazards, including avalanches triggered by extreme snowfall events and flooding caused by rapid snowmelt.

The recent Nepal disaster could be related to a spell of unusually warm weather. This may have weakened the snowpack, creating rapid melt. I work with a team of glaciologists at the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10 km) from the site. Results suggest that enhanced melting could have introduced water into the crevasses, weakening the ice-rock connections.

Studies project that roughly half of the glacier ice in the Himalayas (equivalent to about 2 billion Olympic swimming pools) could melt by the end of this century—enough to raise sea level by more than 1 centimeter. But there is still considerable uncertainty in these projections.

This is because we do not have enough measurements of snowfall and ice across large areas of this challenging terrain. As a result, scientists often have to extrapolate from relatively small numbers of observations to enormous and highly varied terrain.

Computer-based tools (known as models) that combine available observations with information about land and the atmosphere have proved indispensable and often come to the rescue when gap-filling is necessary. But models are only as good as the observations used to constrain them.

New scientific approaches are beginning to offer solutions, but data remain rather sparse and insufficient on their own beyond the regions where they have been tested.

For example, my recent study with colleagues found a new way to accurately measure mountain snowfall, dramatically reducing measurement errors. Measuring snow has been a long-standing problem, which has led mountain water resources to be hugely underestimated over the years.

Another regional study recently reported a measure of the water stored in some of the key Nepalese glaciers using an airborne method involving an aerial survey of the region using instruments mounted on a helicopter. Scientists are also using a technique known as radar interferometry, which uses a combination of radio waves to detect very fast-moving mountain slopes at risk of collapsing.

A combination of one or more such techniques could be used to predict where snowfall is concentrated, how much water it is likely to contribute to the region and areas at risk. New information could inform early warning preparedness strategies, feeding into a forewarning system for the timely evacuation of the region's most vulnerable people.

What happens next?

Scientific innovation alone will not be enough. There is an urgent need for proven ideas to be commercially adapted and systematically deployed across critical zones. The numbers and imminent dangers involved can no longer be confined to discussions in research papers and conferences. They must be made public on the equivalent of a war footing.

An evacuation success story from the Swiss village of Blatten in 2025 shows what this can achieve. Hundreds of people were moved out before a huge section of the glacier broke off. The authorities had already identified areas at risk and publicly shared hazard maps. Continuous monitoring of the landscape, precipitation and ground movement fed into an early warning system.

But success stories from the West cannot simply be transplanted wholesale into the Himalayan context because of the region's inhospitable elevation, harsh weather and limited infrastructure. An approach that factors in indigenous and traditional knowledge should be part of plans and policies.

What is also needed in the Himalayas is a far more highly coordinated monitoring network that brings together everyone who depends on and manages mountain water. This would include state and nonstate organizations, researchers, local authorities and mountain communities. Communities should be central to this effort. Local people can help install and maintain monitoring equipment, collect observations and contribute knowledge of their own environment.

Examples of existing successes from the region include the use of community-managed reservoirs to artificially store meltwater, the construction of ice stupas (an artificial glacier) and glacier grafting techniques to grow new, water-producing glaciers designed to gradually release water during the growing season.

The community-based flood warning system in parts of Nepal's Koshi basin is a success story, but it is limited in its ability to provide alerts during a cascading disaster, such as the one we witnessed recently.

These results should help policymakers and scientists understand how communities dependent on mountain ecosystems are responding to change—and what support they need to adapt and reduce their vulnerability to future hydroclimatic shocks, such as droughts and floods.

Regardless of the current changes in Himalayan snowfall and glacier melt, local people need to play a vital role in helping measure what is happening in the climate system. That, along with countries working more closely together, should help with the desperately needed future planning.

title: How diaspora groups in the US are responding to disasters in Nepal, Colombia, Venezuela and other homelands - phys.org
description: How diaspora groups in the US are responding to disasters in Nepal, Colombia, Venezuela and other homelands  phys.org
publisher.title: phys.org
full_article:
Credit: Israel Torres from Pexels

A string of major disasters in 2026 have had devastating consequences. Earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia and floods and mudslides in Nepal have killed tens of thousands of people and injured many more. Countless people remain missing, and hundreds of thousands of homes are damaged, with some entire neighborhoods destroyed.

The responses have been global. For Nepal alone, the United Nations Global Emergency Fund has allocated US$2 million, while the United States has committed more than $3 million and the European Union has sent just under $3 million. Major humanitarian organizations such as Direct Relief and Save the Children have started fundraising campaigns to support response efforts in Nepal.

Among the first to respond have been support groups set up by people originally from countries hit by disasters but now living elsewhere.

While small in scale, these diaspora groups are well positioned to respond quickly to disasters. They have developed partnerships with community groups on the ground in their home countries. They also have a strong pool of donors—among the diaspora and beyond—in the U.S.

I study philanthropy and nonprofits and research diaspora-led nonprofits. These organizations play multiple roles. They support other people in their immigrant communities in the U.S. and engage in preserving their cultures while living far from their homelands. Increasingly, they also respond to urgent needs in their countries of origin.

Diaspora giving

The money people living abroad send to their relatives and friends back home is called remittances. Globally, more than $900 billion flows across borders annually this way.

Diaspora communities are also playing a growing role in development aid and disaster-response giving in many countries. This is additional money beyond that $900 billion; no authoritative estimate is available.

The Nepalese diaspora groups that have responded are less visible. But nonprofits led by Nepalese people who live in the U.S., like the Nepali Association of Oregon, the Albany New York Nepalese Society and Nepalese Aid, are gathering donations to send back to their homeland.

Likewise, after the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes, Venezuelans living abroad, including business owners, and organizations led by Venezuelan emigrants, such as Venezuelans and Immigrants Aid, have mobilized.

Nonprofits that can step up quickly

My research shows that diaspora-led nonprofits can respond quickly when disasters strike because of the partnerships they have already forged with community groups in their homelands.

For instance, I found that Colombian diaspora-led organizations have ongoing projects in areas ranging from education to nutrition. They can ramp up their philanthropy when a disaster occurs.

Give to Colombia, a nonprofit based in Miami-Dade County and led by Colombians living there, has swiftly dispatched relief funds before. In November 2020, Category 4 Hurricane Iota hit Colombia's Providencia Island. The storm damaged 98% of the island's infrastructure, and an estimated 40% of the 5,000-plus inhabitants were displaced to other parts of the country.

Organizing with its partners, including the Colombian-based nonprofit Presentes Corporation, Give to Colombia created Stand Up: Providencia Reborn. In 2020, the initiative raised $500,000 to build a community center and reconstruct local inns to help more than 1,000 Colombians rebuild their tourism businesses.

Give to Colombia and Presentes Corporation have teamed up again in response to the 7.4-magnitude earthquake that struck the Chocó region of Colombia on Aug. 10, 2026. Together, they have launched Colombia Se Levanta, meaning "Colombia rises up," to raise money to help pay for recovery and rebuilding efforts.

Committed volunteers and donors

Most diaspora-led nonprofits have a committed base of volunteers and donors. In the case of the Albany, New York, Nepalese Society, there are more than 600 Nepalese whom the nonprofit is calling on to give in response to the mudslides.

When I studied Mexican hometown associations, I found that those groups typically had anywhere from 20 to 500 active members, with around 3,000 associations in the United States.

I've also found that diaspora leaders take pride in their philanthropy.

A Colombian immigrant who helped create New England Association for Colombian Children in the Boston area told me, "I do not plan on returning to Colombia now, the U.S. is my home. But I get great fulfillment from giving back to the place where I was born."

She encourages other Colombians living in the U.S. to learn about the organization and give their time and money to causes in Colombia. As a result, the group has become a magnet for many Colombians who end up in the Boston area.

In addition, diaspora-led organizations deliberately involve young immigrants, whether they came to the U.S. as children or were born to immigrant parents.

This can help expand these groups' donor base, even when there's no disaster to respond to. The India Philanthropy Alliance's annual Youth Essay Competition is a good example. It calls on middle and high school students, often Indian Americans, to write essays that identify social challenges facing India and propose solutions.

To be sure, the funds that these diaspora-led nonprofits raise can be modest compared with other efforts. Give to Colombia is close to reaching its target of $300,000 in response to Colombia's 2026 earthquake. The New England Association for Colombian Children also has a campaign underway, Colombia, Estamos Contigo, meaning "We're with you, Colombia." It has already surpassed its target of raising $25,000.

Still, I believe these diaspora-led nonprofits have staying power, given their deep sense of connection with their homelands. They will be ready to respond whenever new disasters occur.

title: Nepal Floods and the impact on animals and communities - worldanimalprotection.org
description: Nepal Floods and the impact on animals and communities  worldanimalprotection.org
publisher.title: worldanimalprotection.org
full_article:
On 26 August 2026, a glacial lake outburst and ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border triggered flash floods and landslides that tore through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors in central Nepal. The disaster devastated districts including Chitwan, Nawalparasi East, Nawalparasi West, Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Tanahu and Gorkha, sweeping away homes, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure. As of the most recent figures from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the death toll in Nepal had climbed past 1,350, with thousands more, including hundreds of foreign nationals and hydropower workers, still missing. Search and rescue operations are ongoing.

Our sympathies are with everyone affected World Animal Protection is deeply saddened by the devastating loss of life and destruction caused by the disaster in Nepal. Our thoughts remain with all those who have lost loved ones, those who have been injured or displaced, and the communities facing the enormous challenges of recovery. The scale of the tragedy has been heartbreaking, and our deepest sympathies are with everyone affected.

Animals: Nepal's hidden victims The devastation caused by this disaster has had a profound impact on animals, who experience fear, pain and distress, just like us. Though the scale of their suffering and loss is all too easy to overlook. In the aftermath of disasters of this scale, animals are extremely vulnerable Cattle, buffalo and goats have been swept away or left stranded without food, clean water or shelter. Treasured companion animals have been separated from their families, while wildlife along the flooded river corridors has been displaced, injured or killed. For people in these communities, this is not only heartbreaking; it can also be devastating to their livelihoods. Losing animals can mean losing income, food and security, often for families with very little to fall back on. Protecting animals and helping them recover is not separate from supporting people; it is an essential part of helping communities rebuild.

A disaster linked to climate change This devastating disaster highlights the growing risks that climate change poses to people, animals and ecosystems. Industrial animal agriculture is a significant driver of this through vast greenhouse gas emissions and deforestation due to its reliance on land for meat production. This is an ineffective and unjust system which also confines billions of sentient animals in inhumane conditions. World Animal Protection believes in order to protect people and animals from the impacts of climate-related disasters we need to end the food systems contributing to the climate crisis.

Supporting the response on the ground In the aftermath of disasters, supporting the people and organisations on the ground is vital to ensuring that animals are cared for during relief and recovery efforts. We greatly value the vital work being undertaken by organisations supporting communities and animals in Nepal. Our colleagues in Denmark are raising funds for the organisations with established resources in Nepal, including: Animal Nepal

Jane Goodall Institute Nepal Voice of Animal Nepal Send your support Our thoughts remain with the people and animals affected, and with everyone working to aid the recovery.

full_article:
Join the Himalaya Sherpa Club of Sonoma for an evening of food, love, and hope in support of Nepal flood disaster relief.

Sonoma Veterans Memorial Hall Sonoma, CA

Tuesday, September 22 • 4:30 PM – 8 PM

For generations, Sonoma has been home to a large, vibrant, and deeply loved Sherpa community; our neighbors, friends, colleagues, and family. Today, many members of this community are directly impacted by the devastating flash floods in Nepal, with loved ones facing unimaginable loss and hardship.

We are hosting a special fundraising dinner to bring our community together in support of those affected in the Rusawa and Nuwakot Region of Nepal. The evening will feature delicious local cuisine, wines and cheeses generously donated by members of our local community.

Admission is free and attendees are encouraged to make a contribution to the disaster relief efforts in support of our local Sherpa brothers and sisters as they do everything they can to bring aid and assistance to those who have lost so much.

This is an opportunity for Sonoma to do what it does best: come together, care for one another, and support our community in times of need.

We hope to see you there!

*All donations will be collected through the California Sherpa Association, a nonprofit organization recognized under Section 501(C3) of the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. The entire amount collected will be consolidated and sent directly to the Government of Nepal Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.

By Sahana Bajracharya

KATHMANDU, Sept 11 (Reuters) - When Sanjay Sah got trapped in a dark tunnel linked to a hydropower station after a devastating flood tore through the structure in Nepal, he was so scared of injuring his eyes on debris that he kept them closed for days. When a miracle rescue happened nine days later, he could barely open them.

"There was nothing for my eyes ‌to see. Most of the time I kept them closed. I was afraid that if I slipped or hit something by mistake, I could injure my eyes. So I kept them shut for long periods," ‌he told Reuters in an exclusive interview after being released from hospital on Friday.

"After doing that repeatedly, it became difficult even to open my eyes again."

Since the collapse of a Himalayan glacier in late August caused devastation in the valleys below, at least 1,300 people have been confirmed ​dead and more than 5,300 are missing across Nepal and China's Tibet region.

Now recovering at his sister's place in Kathmandu, the 30-year-old was a mechanical foreman at the run-of-river Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, owned by the state-run Nepal Electricity Authority, for more than three years.

The multi-storied powerhouse he was stuck in for most of those nine days was built deep inside the mountainside.

Sah said he had no food but drank floodwater and seepage water from the mountain rock.

'WHAT WOULD BE THE POINT OF GIVING UP QUICKLY?'

When despair threatened to overwhelm him, Sah said he turned to the Hindu Maha Mantra, a chant central to Krishna devotion: "Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare."

"Even if I had ‌to die, I thought, what would be the point of giving up quickly? So ⁠I continued to chant God's name and recite the Maha Mantra," Sah recalled. "The Maha Mantra gave me a different kind of feeling, almost a spiritual experience. I wasn't afraid. Instead, I felt calm and relaxed."

From the fifth floor of the six-floor powerhouse, there was an opening through which he could look down and shout, trying to find out if anyone else ⁠was alive. No one responded.

"At the beginning, I was very confident that a rescue would come. Even as the days passed, that confidence remained. I kept telling myself that I was not alone. I had a family, and they would be suffering greatly outside," said Sah, father to a 2-year-old girl, whose wife is 26 years old.

"Thinking about them gave me strength and raised my morale. Even if I was destined to die, I thought, what would be the point of giving up quickly in panic? So I ​kept ​reciting God's name and praying."

He said he had no idea he got rescued only on the 10th day.

"I had completely lost track ​of time and felt as if I had been living in another world," he said. "My ‌guess was that only two or three days had passed. I was shocked when I learned it had actually been 10 days."

He said that in the darkness, he would often bump into things, cut himself on debris or get scraped. Broken tube lights and other objects had fallen around the area, and some of them pierced his feet.

The flood had buried the tunnel under layers of mud and debris, transforming it completely.

"Before the flood I knew every part of it and could have gone deep inside without difficulty. But after the flood, the entire structure had been transformed," he said. "Equipment had been swept away, boxes were scattered everywhere, walls had collapsed and debris had created mounds and pits. My familiarity with the tunnel was no longer useful."

STAYING PUT

He initially tried to move around, but when he realised that he could instead get trapped in an even more difficult place, he stayed put.

"So I turned back and stayed where I ‌believed it was safest," he said. "That is where they eventually found me. Otherwise, I don't know what might have happened to me."

He ​said he would hear sounds from outside in the final hours before rescue.

"I knew they would come. I knew a rescue operation would ​be launched," he said. "I could hear some sounds, like the rumbling of drums. On the day I was ​rescued, and about 10 to 12 hours before that, once things had quietened down a bit, I started hearing noises from outside."

He said: "I could hear the excavators working and the clanging ‌of ladders. About 10 to 12 hours before the rescue, I could clearly hear ​people working. That gave me real hope."

Kabir Maharjan, 45 years old, ​was also trapped in the tunnel and hospitalised at the same army facility with more severe injuries. Sah encountered him moments before the flood struck.

"We both had little time left and headed upward instead of going down," Sah said. "We believed that even if a large flood came, it would not reach that high. We had reached the sixth floor when water began entering from below. First came air pressure, then the ​water itself. We got separated in the chaos. My mobile phone was swept away. ‌I do not know where Kabir ended up."

A devotee of Lord Krishna, Sah was rescued on the day when Hindus celebrated the birth of one of their biggest deities.

"That is the saddest part of all," Sah said.

title: 'Chilling': As Nepal Grapples With Flooding Chaos, Christians Face Another Potential Horror - cbn.com
description: 'Chilling': As Nepal Grapples With Flooding Chaos, Christians Face Another Potential Horror  cbn.com
publisher.title: cbn.com
full_article:
As Nepal deals with the horrific toll of tragic flooding that killed more than 1,000 people, at least 20 churches have reportedly been destroyed by the damaging waters.

Joel Veldkamp, head of international communications at Christian Solidarity International (CSI), told CBN News that one congregation has 80 individuals and families who lost their homes — and that’s just one example.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

CSI has been working to get food, mattresses, mosquito nets, cleaning supplies, and other items to people in Nepal to help meet basic needs.

Veldkamp said there’s another dynamic unfolding inside the South Asian nation: persecution, an issue gaining steam and attention before the deadly flooding began.

“We’ve seen in the last 10 years … persecution of Christians has spiked in Nepal,” he said. “It wasn’t really a big problem before, and today it’s still not on the scale like we’ll see in India, or Pakistan, or other nearby countries. But there is now a law against conversion, so it’s illegal to try to get someone else to change their religion.”

Veldkamp said this is a violation of human rights standards, but that this law is used to prosecute pastors and missionaries — even Christians who might happen to visit and speak with Hindu friends.

“We have seen an uptick in these cases of Christians being jailed on accusations,” he said, noting that sharing the Gospel can be enough to spark legal chaos.

Veldkamp said there’s a new government in Nepal after the previous regime was overthrown in a revolution. An election unfolded in March, which has only added to the uncertainty.

“We still don’t know really what that means, but the country is in flux [and] is headed in a new political direction,” he said. “There are some good signs and some bad signs from the new government, so Christians in Nepal are very concerned about which way the country is going to go now.”

Nepal is one of two Hindu-majority nations in the world, with India joining it in that distinction. Until 2008, Nepal was a Hindu nation before becoming a federal republic. Today, there are new calls to return to that previous designation — something that should be of concern to Christians and other religious minorities.

India has been reportedly putting pressure on Nepal to embrace Hindu nationalism, funding groups that seek to push Christians to reconvert, among other issues.

“There are serious efforts to change Nepal’s constitution to make it officially a Hindu country again,” Veldkamp said. “And in the current environment, that would mean probably the harassment of Christians. Attacks on churches would only increase because then it would be official that this country does not belong to Christians.”

With pastors, missionaries, and Christians already under fire, he said there’s a “real threat that is having a chilling effect” on believers in Nepal.

“Right now, when these things happen to Christians, Christians can say, ‘Hey, we’re a secular country. Nepal is a country for everyone. It says so in our Constitution,'” Veldkamp said. “And that’s … a good argument. That’s a good lever that they can use to appeal to their fellow Nepali citizens for justice.”

But if Nepal becomes a Hindu nation, these arguments dissipate both legally and in the public sphere. Veldkamp encouraged believers worldwide to pray for the church.

title: DJI FlyCart 100s Feed Nepal Flood Survivors As US Taxes Them 100% - DroneXL
description: DJI FlyCart 100s Feed Nepal Flood Survivors As US Taxes Them 100%  DroneXL
publisher.title: DroneXL
full_article:
Tracker Drone Delivery Tracker: every US operator, hub and incident on the record

Nepal’s army is flying four DJI FlyCart 100 cargo drones, all donated by China, on 10 to 16 relief runs a day across the Trishuli River, two weeks after the government asked foreign governments for exactly that kind of aircraft. The drones carry up to 132 pounds (60 kg) of food, medicine and fuel per trip to villages that lost their roads and bridges on Aug. 26, and drones have also carried bodies out of areas rescuers cannot reach on foot.

The official toll stood at 1,369 dead and 5,132 missing in Nepal as of Sept. 9, among them 587 foreign nationals. Chinese officials count 43 dead and 519 missing on the Tibetan side.

The aircraft doing the lifting is one the United States put in a 100% tariff bracket on Sept. 3, eight days after the glacier broke, and one the Federal Communications Commission proposes to bar from American sale outright.

Nepal’s Army Flies Four Donated FlyCart 100s From Devighat

The four FlyCart 100s arrived in a Chinese aid package and now fly relief across the Trishuli from Devighat in Nuwakot district, Reuters reported on Sept. 9. Each run covers 2 to 2.5 miles (3 to 4 km) with up to 132 pounds (60 kg) of food, medicine and fuel.

“There is no other way to send food, essentials, medicine and fuel, except for drones,” contract army pilot Santosh Budhathoki told Reuters, because the army’s helicopters are tied up in rescue. Milan Pandey of Airlift Technology, the Nepali operator whose crews DroneXL has followed since they replaced Sherpa porters on the Khumbu Icefall in 2024, is running the flights, and told Reuters the crews have been shuttling since early morning.

That closes the question DroneXL left open on Aug. 30, when Nepal had run one schoolyard test flight and asked abroad for heavy-lift drones while China had 47 drones flying on its side of the border. Beijing answered with the heaviest aircraft on the scene. India’s Garuda Aerospace also sent pilots and its Sanjeevani logistics drones, rated for 55 pounds (25 kg), to Rasuwa district, the company said, less than half of what one FlyCart run carries.

The DJI Flycart 100 lowers supplies via winch line to a flood-stricken area in Nepal as onlookers watch. Photo credit: Nepal Photo Library.

By Sept. 9 drones had delivered 1,591 kilograms (3,508 pounds) of food to cut-off villages, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, whose situation report also carries the death and missing figures. Reuters reported that drones have moved flood victims’ bodies in some areas, and reconnaissance drones have been in constant use for search and rescue.

DJI Rates The FlyCart 100 At 187 Pounds And Nepal Flies It At 132

DJI’s own spec sheet rates the FlyCart 100 for 187 pounds (85 kg) on two batteries and 220 pounds (100 kg) on one, hung from a 98-foot (30 m) winch line. Nepal’s crews load 132 pounds (60 kg), a margin that buys range and wind tolerance.

A DJI Flycart 100 lowers a supply container on a winch line while delivering aid in flood-stricken Nepal. Photo credit: Nepal Photo Library.

DJI launched the aircraft globally on Dec. 4, 2025, and DroneXL walked through its sensor stack at the time: LiDAR, front and rear radar, a quad-vision system, a parachute, and an IP55 rating for dust and rain. The same model spent the spring hauling 22,207 pounds (10,073 kg) of cargo between Everest Base Camp and Camp 1, work DroneXL covered in July, which is why Nepal already had licensed pilots for it when the flood came.

DJI’s payload figures are measured at sea level in still air, and the spec sheet says capacity falls with takeoff altitude. Devighat sits low in the valley, well below where that derating bites on DJI’s own numbers, so the gap between 60 and 85 kilograms is operating margin, not the aircraft’s limit.

Small Drones Search Hydropower Tunnels Packed With Mud

Away from the cargo runs, thermal drones are hunting for roughly 900 workers still missing from 12 hydropower projects, about 500 of them believed to be inside plant tunnels, the Associated Press reported. The flood filled some tunnels end to end. A drone can only fly the straight ones.

Filmmaker and drone pilot Manish Maharjan joined the army’s search a day after the flood and told the AP that at the Rasuwagadhi hydropower project he flew a drone to the end of the tunnel and found no air pocket at all. “We found tunnels were filled with mud like toothpaste in a tube,” he said. Bends and zigzags stop the search where the signal drops.

On open hillsides the same drones did better. Maharjan mounted speakers on them to call out to stranded people and play music, and helped rescue teams find survivors that way in the first days after the flood.

Washington Put A 100% Tariff On This Aircraft Eight Days After The Flood

President Trump’s Aug. 13 proclamation put a 100% tariff on imported drones with a maximum takeoff weight above 55 pounds (25 kg), effective Sept. 3. The FlyCart 100 takes off at 330 pounds (149.9 kg). Each of the four aircraft feeding Nuwakot clears that bar six times over.

DroneXL reported the proclamation the day it was signed. One day before the tariff started, on Sept. 2, public comments closed on the FCC’s proposal to end U.S. sales of thermal, LiDAR, docking, spraying and heavy-lift drones it had previously approved, a proceeding DroneXL has tracked since the commission put every foreign drone on the Covered List in December 2025.

The American alternative has been to Nepal and back. This spring the Home Ministry refused Freefly a permit to fly its Alta X Gen 2 on Everest and suspended Airlift’s FlyCart 100 permit in the same stroke; the DJI permit came back in five days, the Freefly one never did, and Airlift flew the Alta X on Ama Dablam instead in June, with the U.S. Embassy applauding. Pandey told The Wall Street Journal, per Ars Technica, that at Everest altitudes the DJI aircraft lifts about 100 pounds to the Freefly’s 11, and costs less. The embassy’s July post on the Ama Dablam flights gave no payload figure.

DroneXL’s Take

Nepal asked the world for heavy-lift drones on Aug. 29. China had four in the air by Sept. 4, the date on the first AFP frames from Trishuli, and they are the best aircraft in the class. That is the whole story, and it is a story about the United States.

I want to be fair to Beijing’s motives, because they are not charitable. Four FlyCarts over Rasuwa are soft power at a price DJI can write off, and China gets to be the country whose drones fed the survivors while its own side of the border counts 519 missing. Nobody in Washington should mistake this for altruism. But the American answer to a donated DJI aircraft doing good work cannot be a customs bill and a docket to ban it, because that answer leaves the next Nepal with the same choice and one fewer bidder.

The tariff, as I see it, protects no one who builds anything. Freefly makes a serious heavy lifter in Washington State, Blue-listed and NDAA-compliant, and Nepal still would not let it fly Everest. The 100% rate does not fix that. It raises the price of the aircraft an American county emergency manager would buy tomorrow if a river took the bridge, and it does so while the FCC weighs whether that manager may buy it at all. Protecting a domestic industry means giving it stages to prove itself on, which is what Ama Dablam was. Taxing the competitor out of the country while the competitor donates aircraft to the disaster of the year is how you lose the argument in front of the people who decide it.

The number I keep coming back to is 11 pounds. If Pandey’s figure holds, and it is one operator’s account relayed through the Journal, the American aircraft lifts a tenth of the Chinese one at altitude. That is an engineering gap, not a policy gap, and no tariff closes it. What closes it is the thing DroneXL has argued for since the FlyCart 30 first flew Everest: American companies competing on the same mountains, in the same disasters, on merit. Nepal’s next request will come after the next glacier. Whether an American aircraft is on the list of what arrives is the question worth watching, and the FCC’s answer to its own docket will decide part of it.

Sources: Reuters (via CBC News), Associated Press, Nepal NDRRMA situation report, DJI, Ars Technica

title: Northern Virginia holds vigil for Nepal flood victims - Diya TV
description: Northern Virginia holds vigil for Nepal flood victims  Diya TV
publisher.title: Diya TV
full_article:
SOUTH RIDING, Va. (Diya TV) — Residents, elected officials and religious leaders gathered at South Riding Town Green in Loudoun County for an interfaith candlelight vigil honoring victims of the Nepal floods and those who remain missing.

Some attendees carried photographs of missing relatives and friends as representatives of several faiths offered prayers and participants observed moments of silence.

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., said several people reported missing have ties to Virginia, including residents of Loudoun County. He told IANS that he personally knew some of them.

Subramanyam said his office has been in regular contact with the State Department regarding the search for missing U.S. citizens and residents.

“Our team is talking to them virtually every day,” Subramanyam said.

A local community representative said seven Loudoun County residents remained missing at the time of the vigil. Families and community members have also been holding nightly calls to exchange information, according to IANS.

The United States has provided humanitarian and disaster-response assistance to Nepal following the Aug. 26 floods. Two U.S. military cargo aircraft delivered thousands of disaster-recovery supplies, first-aid kits, stretchers and heavy equipment earlier this month to support Nepal-led search and recovery operations.

U.S. officials have also been working with families on DNA collection to assist with the identification of recovered remains, Subramanyam said. Families of missing people from several countries have provided DNA samples as identification efforts continue.

Subramanyam joined Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi, Ro Khanna and other lawmakers last week in urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to provide additional resources for search-and-rescue operations and assistance to Americans affected by the disaster.

title: Providing Relief to Flood-Ravaged Communities in Nepal - Samaritan's Purse
description: Providing Relief to Flood-Ravaged Communities in Nepal  Samaritan's Purse
publisher.title: Samaritan's Purse
full_article:
Samaritan’s Purse is working through trusted partners to distribute relief to families affected by the unprecedented flash flooding that killed hundreds and displaced thousands in Nepal.

Narayan was at home eating breakfast with his family when he received a phone call from a friend who told him that a major flood was headed toward his hometown of Devighat. A chicken farmer by trade, he peered out the window at his coops below and watched the Trishuli river start to rise.

Narayan had to flee his home with his family. His house and livelihood were swept away.

“At first, the river started overflowing slowly, but within two minutes, my entire poultry farm was completely swept away by the flood,” he said. “That’s when we realized we couldn’t stay home any longer.”

Narayan ushered his family out the door and fled with them to higher ground. They watched as the raging floodwaters not only washed away his livelihood of 1,300 chickens, but also destroyed the two-story home where he had raised his two children.

Meeting Critical Needs

The August 26 flash flood was triggered by a major glacial collapse near the Nepal–China border. It pushed a tidal wave south along the Lende Khola and Trishuli̇ Khola rivers. What at first looked like a black cloud quickly became a surging dark wall of water, rock, and ice.

Samaritan’s Purse teams and local partners invited residents to gather supplies delivered to the country by our 767 cargo plane.

Gaining speed and momentum, the avalanche-like floodwaters swelled and traveled over 60 miles, affecting multiple northern Nepali districts and claiming more than 1,400 lives.

“Little by little, all the money I’d earned over so many years was lost,” Narayan said. “I have to start again from zero.”

In response to the catastrophic event, Samaritan’s Purse deployed a team of disaster relief specialists who began coordinating with local authorities and Christian partners on the ground to provide relief in Jesus’ Name. In addition to procuring supplies locally, our 767-cargo plane landed in Nepal carrying over 80,000 pounds of relief, including hygiene kits, solar lights, water filters, and more.

Residents of the region have a long recovery ahead of them.

“These villages have been absolutely decimated,” said Darren Tosh, Samaritan’s Purse team lead. “So, we are here to be able to start to bring some hope back to those communities with some emergency relief.”

Working through several Christian groups and churches, teams began hosting distributions throughout three of the hardest hit districts.

“Our partners have an ambition to be able to serve these communities in Jesus’ Name, being a witness through their actions and through their compassion as they end up helping these families recover,” Tosh said.

When Narayan arrived at a distribution hosted by one our partners, he was thankful to receive shelter plastic, a blanket, hygiene kit, and solar light, among other items.

Narayan was especially grateful for a water filter and jerry bucket, as his family had no access to clean water for several days after the flood.

“We had a reserve tank we had for the chickens, and we drank that water for six days,” he said. “The water filter will be helpful.”

Having served in the Nepali army for 17 years, Narayan is determined to stay strong for his family and rebuild their future.

“I am not defeated,” he said. “I can get back up again.”

Devanand Kadariya is with Nepal Baptist Church Council, one of our trusted partners. He also serves on Nepal’s national leadership team with Operation Christmas Child, a Samaritan’s Purse project.

For him, meeting with beneficiaries like Narayan is an opportunity to tangibly demonstrate the love of Christ.

“We love people as Christ loves people, whether they’re Christian or not Christian,” Kadariya said. “It’s our duty to love our neighbor as ourselves, and this is an opportunity to go and help people in need.”

Hope for the Weary

Rameswori deeply misses the home she once had in the city of Bhaise, Nepal. She was alone when the unprecedented 30-foot wall of water ravaged her hometown, killing two of her relatives.

Rameswori is grateful for the help of God’s people as she continues to remember the devastating flooding.

“I dream about the flood every night, and I have fear in my heart whenever I have that dream,” she said.

At first, Rameswori didn’t believe her sister when she said the waters were coming her way, but when she eventually made her way outside, the water was already rising.

“When the flood got close, I stepped outside and everyone had already left the area and gone somewhere safe,” she said. “I did my best to get away from there and managed to reach the road.”

For years, Rameswori had been dealing with knee pain and had also recently fractured her foot, so she was grateful when a neighbor grabbed her hand and helped her to higher ground. She watched as the flash flood swept her home away.

“My house was a very beautiful house–full of gardens, full of flowers. It was like a resort,” she said. “Remembering that house, my heart breaks all over again.”

Rameswori needed more than physical relief; she also needed encouragement. When she arrived at one of our distributions, she was grateful to receive both.

“The support that the flood victims and I received today has given us hope,” she said. The essential aid was a reminder that her community had not been forgotten. “It has given relief to us and our people. So, we are very thankful.”

Encouraging the Body of Christ

The catastrophic flash flood came just over 10 years after the Himalayan nation was rocked by a 7.8-magnitude earthquake that killed around 9,000 people. Samaritan’s Purse immediately responded with critical aid and medical support, and stayed for three years helping communities rebuild, including Pastor Ishwor’s new church.

Water, mud, and debris covered towns in the narrow valleys.

“I have been praying that Samaritan’s Purse would come back again and help,” said Ishwor Pudasaini, who has been pastoring a church in the Nuwakot District for 25 years.

“When our church collapsed during the earthquake, Samaritan’s Purse helped by sending volunteers and the materials for a new church building,” he said. “Not only did they help our church, but they helped the community outside the church as well.”

When Pastor Ishwor learned that Samaritan’s Purse was coming to Devighat–the city he grew up in–to distribute relief items and share the hope of Jesus Christ, he was relieved to know he was not alone.

“As a pastor and a leader of my church who is worried about this community, I am very grateful when I meet people like Samaritan’s Purse, because it gives me the confidence and the courage to fight against this crisis,” he said. “And I know that I am not alone in restoring this community.”

Please pray as our partners continue to reach flood-ravaged communities, providing hope and relief in Jesus’ Name.

title: Nepal flood disaster exposes cascading threats in Himalayas - phys.org
description: Nepal flood disaster exposes cascading threats in Himalayas  phys.org
publisher.title: phys.org
full_article:
Many homes and infrastructure near the Bhotekoshi River were damaged or destroyed during the devastating flash floods that left thousands of people missing. Credit: Gautam/UNICEF

A catastrophic flood in Nepal that left thousands missing began with a collapse of ice and rock high in the mountains—a warning that disaster planning must prepare for chains of hazards, not isolated events, experts say.

The cascade of ice, rock and debris that tumbled through the Nepal–China border region last week probably blocked a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, forming a dam before bursting downstream with devastating force, according to disaster analysis.

The torrent arrived in Nepal's Rasuwa district with little warning, ripping through settlements along the Bhotekoshi River system, destroying bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure and cutting a vital trade route with Tibet.

More than 1,000 people have been confirmed dead, with almost 4,000 still missing and around 11,800 rescued, according to UN figures on Tuesday (Sept. 1). Thousands are in need of humanitarian assistance, hindered by blocked roads and damaged bridges.

Experts say the disaster illustrates a growing problem across the Hindu Kush Himalaya: hazards that once might have been assessed separately—glacier collapse, landslides, avalanches, river blockages, floods and even earthquakes—can interact within minutes or hours, creating an event much larger than any one of them.

"Most people think of flash floods as being caused by heavy rainfall," said Liz Stephens, professor of climate risks and resilience at the University of Reading in the UK.

But in high-mountain regions, such floods can result from "complex chains of hazards, including landslides, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods," she added.

That complexity, Stephens says, makes early warning particularly difficult.

Tributary blocked

Analysis of satellite imagery from U.S. aerospace and data analytics company Planet Labs suggests that a substantial section of glacier and surrounding rock collapsed at high altitude near the Nepal–China border, sending an enormous mass of ice, snow and debris toward the valley.

The collapse appears to have affected the Lhende Khola, a tributary that becomes part of the Bhotekoshi River system.

A rapid-analysis report released by the Integrated Research on Disaster Risk (IRDR) on Friday (Aug. 28) said the event was likely caused by an "ice, rock and soil mass failure" rather than intense rainfall.

The material probably blocked the river for about 18 or 19 hours, forming a natural dam that then gave way on the morning of Aug. 26, unleashing masses of water, ice, rocks and sediment, the report said.

Funneled by the steep Himalayan terrain, the surge became a fast-moving mixture of water and debris capable of carrying huge boulders, destroying bridges and erasing riverbanks.

The rapid-analysis report said the steep gradient and narrow valley accelerated and concentrated the flow, while the heavy debris load increased its destructive power.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said the flood was "caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming" and described this as a "new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters" on the Tibetan Plateau.

"Bigger than the atom bomb"

Experts say these findings highlight the need for change in disaster monitoring.

A conventional flood warning system may detect rising rainfall or river levels. But a cascading cryospheric event can begin kilometers away, and at much higher elevation, with no obvious warning for communities downstream.

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) argues that disaster planning in the region needs to move away from treating hazards independently.

"With the nature of disaster risks rapidly mutating in the region, disaster risk reduction strategies can no longer evaluate hazards in isolation," Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at ICIMOD, said.

"The era of preparing for a single, predictable hazard is over."

The disaster comes just over a year after another major flood affected the same Lhende Khola–Bhotekoshi system.

In July 2025, flooding in the area was linked by Nepali authorities to a glacial lake outburst. The recurrence is raising questions about whether the river corridor is becoming a particularly exposed pathway for cryosphere-related hazards.

A 2026 ICIMOD assessment found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya lost about 12% of their area between 1990 and 2020, and the rate of ice loss has doubled since 2000.

As glaciers retreat, new lakes can form, slopes can lose the support provided by ice, and frozen ground can become unstable. A glacier collapse can then entrain rock and soil, turning an initial ice avalanche into a debris flow capable of traveling tens of kilometers.

Research published in April on Himalayan hanging glaciers found that rising temperatures and shifting regional precipitation patterns are reducing glacier stability and increasing the risk of ice avalanches. The authors identified more than 219 hanging glaciers in northern India's Alaknanda basin and warned that break-offs can cause physical damage and trigger secondary hazards, including glacial lake outburst floods.

A separate study on ice-rock avalanches in the Himalayas similarly concluded that such failures can rapidly transform into high-velocity debris flows, while stressing the difficulty of identifying precursors, or warning signs.

Geohazard expert Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of Tribhuvan University's Centre for Disaster Studies in Nepal, described the Aug. 26 flood as an unprecedented event in the region.

"In my research career, I haven't seen a bigger flood event than this in the Himalayan landscape," Adhikari said, attributing its extraordinary force to the enormous volume of ice and debris that descended from the mountains.

"I calculated the amount of energy, which is bigger than the atom bomb that happened in Hiroshima," he added.

He said the scale of the event demonstrates the immense destructive potential of cascading ice, rock and water hazards in the Himalayas.

Neighbors at risk

The disaster also raises questions about disaster preparedness in the wider region.

The Hindu Kush Himalaya stretches across Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, as well as Nepal and the Tibetan Plateau, connecting communities through river systems that cross political boundaries.

In India, the 2021 Chamoli disaster demonstrated the destructive potential of a similar ice-rock cascade. A massive collapse in Uttarakhand sent water, ice and debris through the Rishiganga Valley, killing more than 200 people and destroying hydropower facilities.

Scientists are increasingly treating such events as compound hazards rather than isolated disasters.

Across Bhutan and Nepal, glacial lakes are being monitored for possible outburst floods. In Pakistan, rapidly changing glaciers and high-mountain valleys create a complex combination of flood, landslide and avalanche risks.

A recent UNDP assessment of human security in the Hindu Kush Himalaya warned that climate impacts can cascade across interconnected food, water and energy systems, creating compound threats greater than individual hazards considered separately.

Satellite warnings

Experts say the Rasuwa disaster also provides a powerful demonstration of the potential—and limits—of satellite technology.

Satellite images helped scientists reconstruct what happened in an otherwise extremely difficult-to-access area. High-resolution imagery can reveal changes in glacier geometry, newly formed lakes, landslide scars, blocked rivers and altered drainage channels.

In the aftermath of the flood, authorities have used satellite observations to monitor newly formed lakes upstream that could pose additional risks if their natural barriers fail.

But identifying a disaster after it happens is very different from predicting it beforehand.

Ishfaq Ahmad, a satellite scientist based in Nepal, told SciDev.Net that while scientists can identify and assess potentially dangerous glacial lakes using satellite imagery and visual observations, predicting the exact moment when a lake will burst remains a challenge.

"Glacial lakes can be seen with our eyes and through satellite data. We can assess whether the lakes are potentially dangerous or not," Ahmad said.

But he said sudden triggers, such as rockfalls or ice collapses, can occur too rapidly for orbiting satellites to detect them in advance.

Satellites do not continuously observe every Himalayan slope at the resolutions needed to reliably detect an imminent collapse. Clouds can obscure optical imagery, while revisit times can leave gaps between useful observations.

Ground sensors can provide continuous measurements, but installing and maintaining them is challenging in remote, high-altitude terrain, where field observations remain sparse.

The answer, therefore, is unlikely to be a single technology.

Scientists increasingly argue for combining satellite imagery with seismic sensors, river gauges, automated cameras, weather forecasts, glacier monitoring and local community warning networks.

ICIMOD has noted that only a fraction of Himalayan glaciers are adequately monitored, leaving large areas as blind spots. It has called for better data and for scientific information to be translated into decisions that communities can act on.
